power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p = .345", "p = .059", "p = .258"), Sentence = c("For DUIC avoidance, sex moderated the direct association between descriptive norms and avoidance (b = 0.397, 95% CI [0.106, 0.688], p = .008), which was significant among men (b = 0.509, p < .001) but not among women (b = 0.112, p = .345; Figure 2).", "Sex did not moderate the association between descriptive norms and self-efficacy (p = .059) or between self-efficacy and avoidance (p = .258), and the conditional indirect effects did not differ between men and women (difference = 0.033, 95% CI [-0.099, 0.140]).", "Sex did not moderate the association between descriptive norms and self-efficacy (p = .059) or between self-efficacy and avoidance (p = .258), and the conditional indirect effects did not differ between men and women (difference = 0.033, 95% CI [-0.099, 0.140])." )), row.names = c(NA, -3L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

text.text: Simultaneous alcohol and cannabis use (SAC) and driving under the influence of cannabis (DUIC) are prevalent risk behaviors among young adults who use cannabis.
Drawing on social cognitive theory, we expected that perceiving peers´ avoidance of these behaviors would strengthen confidence to avoid them.
This prospective study examined whether self-efficacy mediated the association between descriptive norms and SAC and DUIC avoidance, and whether these associations differed by sex.

From 505 young adults who completed baseline and 3-month follow-up assessments, two samples were drawn: participants who used alcohol and cannabis (n = 382; Mage = 21.03; 39.3% women) and those who used cannabis and drove (n = 167; Mage = 21.70; 31.7% women) at both time points.
Controlling for sex, age, university status, and baseline risk behavior, higher descriptive norms and self-efficacy were associated with greater avoidance of both behaviors.

Self-efficacy mediated the association between norms and avoidance of both behaviors, and neither the association between norms and selfefficacy nor the indirect association differed significantly by sex.
Sex moderated only the association between norms and DUIC avoidance, which was significant among men.
Normative feedback interventions highlighting peers´ avoidance could target both perceived norms and self-efficacy, especially for DUIC among men.
Cannabis remains the most widely used illicit substance worldwide and is particularly prevalent among young adults (United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime [UNODC], 2022 [UNODC], , 2024)).

text.text: Among young adults who use cannabis, two risk behaviors are especially prevalent: simultaneous alcohol and cannabis use (SAC, reported by roughly half of those use both substances (Subbaraman & Kerr, 2015), and driving under the influence of cannabis (DUIC; Lloyd et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Among young adults who use cannabis, two risk behaviors are especially prevalent: simultaneous alcohol and cannabis use (SAC, reported by roughly half of those use both substances <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">(Subbaraman & Kerr, 2015)</ref>, and driving under the influence of cannabis (DUIC; <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Lloyd et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: SAC refers to the overlapping psychoactive effects of both alcohol and cannabis.

Compared with using each substance separately, simultaneous use has been associated with heavier consumption of both alcohol and cannabis (Sokolovsky et al., 2020), as well as with greater health-related harms, including comorbid alcohol use disorder and mental health problems, memory blackouts, academic difficulties, and increased subjective intoxication (Cummings et al., 2019; Yurasek et al., 2017).

text.text: DUIC likewise represents a major public health concern: acute cannabis intoxication impairs driving performance and has been linked to elevated crash risk (Favretto et al., 2023; Lane & Hall, 2019; Simmons et al., 2022).

text.text: Given these risks, identifying the psychosocial factors associated with the avoidance of SAC and DUIC may inform the development of interventions to prevent these behaviors among young adults who use cannabis.
Descriptive norms and self-efficacy are two well-established psychosocial determinants of health-related behaviors (Albarracín et al., 2024; Papakonstantinou et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Descriptive norms and self-efficacy are two well-established psychosocial determinants of health-related behaviors <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Albarracín et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Papakonstantinou et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: In the substance use field, both have been consistently identified as relevant explanatory factors of alcohol and cannabis use (Chen et al., 2022; Walker et al., 2011), and more specifically of the protective behaviors that reduce substance-related harm (Arterberry et al., 2014; Fairlie et al., 2021; Fernández-Calderón et al., 2022).

text.text: In this context, perceived descriptive norms refer to beliefs about how frequently peers engage in each behavior (Borsari & Carey, 2001 , 2003; Napper et al., 2016).

text.text: Perceived norms regarding peers' use of protective behavioral strategies have been associated with individuals' own protective practices among young adults who use alcohol and cannabis (Arterberry et al., 2014; Fairlie et al., 2021; Fernández-Calderón et al., 2022; Romero-Pérez et al., 2026).

text.text: Descriptive norms have also been linked to greater engagement in SAC (Boyle et al., 2023; Coelho et al., 2025), whereas evidence concerning cannabisimpaired driving is more mixed (Hultgren et al., 2024).

text.text: However, whether descriptive norms are also associated with the adoption of the corresponding protective behaviorsnamely, avoiding SAC and DUIC-remains largely unexamined.
To our knowledge, no study has specifically assessed descriptive norms for avoiding SAC or DUIC in relation to their subsequent adoption.

Self-efficacy, defined as the belief in one's capacity to execute the specific behaviors required to achieve desired outcomes (Bandura, 1997), constitutes wellestablished proximal determinant of health-related behaviors and a core construct in major social cognitive models, including social cognitive theory (Bandura, 1977), protection motivation theory (Rogers, 1983), and the theory of planned behavior (Ajzen, 1991).
text.formatted: Self-efficacy, defined as the belief in one's capacity to execute the specific behaviors required to achieve desired outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Bandura, 1997)</ref>, constitutes wellestablished proximal determinant of health-related behaviors and a core construct in major social cognitive models, including social cognitive theory <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Bandura, 1977)</ref>, protection motivation theory <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Rogers, 1983)</ref>, and the theory of planned behavior <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Ajzen, 1991)</ref>.

text.text: Previous research has consistently shown that higher self-efficacy to refuse substance use is linked to lower alcohol and cannabis use (González-Ponce et al., 2026; Jang et al., 2013; Parrado-González et al., 2025), as well as to a lower likelihood of driving under the influence of substances (El Hafidy et al., 2024; Hai et al., 2024; Somoray et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Previous research has consistently shown that higher self-efficacy to refuse substance use is linked to lower alcohol and cannabis use <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(González-Ponce et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Jang et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Parrado-González et al., 2025)</ref>, as well as to a lower likelihood of driving under the influence of substances <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(El Hafidy et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Hai et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Somoray et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: By contrast, perceived self-efficacy to enact protective behaviors has received comparatively less attention, and the available evidence is mixed.

Selfefficacy has been associated with the use of, or intention to use, protective strategies in some studies (González-Ponce et al., 2024; Pearson & Bravo, 2019), but not when other the constructs of the theory of planned behavior were considered (Fernández-Calderón et al., 2025; Vera et al., 2025).

text.text: In particular, the only study examining SAC avoidance, conducted with the same cohort, found no association with self-efficacy (Vera et al., 2025), and, to our knowledge, no study has yet examined the role of self-efficacy in DUIC avoidance.

text.text: Beyond its direct association with behavior, social cognitive theory posits that self-efficacy beliefs can be acquired through vicarious learning-that is, observing similar others successfully navigate challenging situations (Bandura, 1977 (Bandura, , 1997;; Conner & Norman, 2015).

text.text: From this perspective, descriptive norms may constitute a source of vicarious information: by conveying how frequently peers successfully enact a given behavior, they may strengthen individuals' confidence in their own capacity to do the same.
Accordingly, perceiving that peers frequently avoid SAC and DUIC could enhance self-efficacy for these protective behaviors and, in turn, facilitate their enactment.

Although this pathway is theoretically grounded, whether self-efficacy mediates the association between descriptive norms and protective behavior in the substance use domain remains, to our knowledge, largely unexamined.
On this basis, we tested whether self-efficacy operates as a mediating mechanism linking descriptive norms to SAC and DUIC avoidance.
The social-cognitive mechanisms underlying the adoption of protective behaviors may vary by sex.

Perceiving that peers use protective behavioral strategies has been associated with greater personal use of these strategies, and this positive association has been stronger among men than among women (Romero-Pérez et al., 2026).

text.text: Similarly, higher self-efficacy has been associated with stronger intentions to avoid drink-driving, particularly among men (Moan & Rise, 2011), and perceiving that peers drive under the influence of cannabis has been associated with stronger intentions to do so, especially among men with higher self-efficacy (Earle et al., 2020).

text.text: Drawing on this social-cognitive framework, the present prospective study had three aims: (i) to examine the associations among perceived descriptive norms for avoiding SAC and DUIC, self-efficacy to avoid them, and their personal avoidance in a community-based sample of young adults who use cannabis; (ii) to examine the mediating role of self-efficacy in the relationship between descriptive norms and the avoidance of each behavior; and (iii) to test whether sex moderates both this mediating mechanism and each the association involved (i.e., between descriptive norms and selfefficacy, between self-efficacy and avoidance, between descriptive norms and avoidance).

Building on previous social-cognitive theories, and empirical findings, we anticipate that young adults with high perceived descriptive norm and self-efficacy for avoiding SAC and DUIC would report greater subsequent avoidance of each behavior (Arterberry et al., 2014; Fairlie et al., 2021; Fernández-Calderón et al., 2022).

text.text: We further hypothesized that higher descriptive norms would relate to greater self-efficacy and, in turn, to greater avoidance (Bandura, 1997; Conner & Norman, 2015).

text.text: Given the limited evidence on sex differences in these associations (Earle et al., 2020; Moan & Rise, 2011; Romero-Pérez et al., 2026), the moderating role of sex was examined in an exploratory manner, without a specific directional hypothesis.

text.text: A targeted sampling strategy (Watters & Biernacki, 1989) was used to recruit young adults residing in two cities in southern Spain (Huelva and Seville) between June 2022 and July 2023.
text.formatted: A targeted sampling strategy <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">(Watters & Biernacki, 1989</ref>) was used to recruit young adults residing in two cities in southern Spain (Huelva and Seville) between June 2022 and July 2023.

text.text: Eligibility criteria were (a) being aged 18-25 years and (b) reporting cannabis use on at least one occasion in the past 30 days.
A total of 616 individuals participated in the study.
Four were excluded due to inconsistent response patterns, resulting in a final baseline sample of 612 young adults (M age= 21.04, SD = 2.16).
Recruitment was conducted across all districts of both cities.
Within each district, settings where young adults typically gather (parks, squares, nightlife areas, bars, and pubs) were identified by consulting young adults who used cannabis.
Three field researchers approached potential participants in these settings (21.0%), and study advertisements were displayed across all districts (46.7%).
In addition, snowball sampling was used, with nominations capped at five per participant to reduce sample homogeneity (32.4%).
Sociodemographic and cannabis use characteristics were monitored throughout recruitment to ensure sample heterogeneity (Thompson & Collins, 2002).
text.formatted: Sociodemographic and cannabis use characteristics were monitored throughout recruitment to ensure sample heterogeneity <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Thompson & Collins, 2002)</ref>.

text.text: A detailed description of the recruitment procedure is available in Sánchez-García et al. (2024).
text.formatted: A detailed description of the recruitment procedure is available in <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Sánchez-García et al. (2024)</ref>.

text.text: Assessments were conducted in person, individually or in small groups of up to five participants, in rooms provided by the University of Huelva and by organizations supporting people who use drugs in Seville.
After providing informed consent and completing the questionnaire, participants received a €15 voucher and provided contact details for the follow-up assessment.
The baseline sample comprised 612 young adults who reported past-month cannabis use.
The follow-up assessment was conducted three months after baseline using mixed-mode contact procedure.

One week before the follow-up window, participants received a WhatsApp prenotification announcing a telephone call to schedule the assessment; nonresponders were recontacted via WhatsApp and then by telephone, and this sequence was repeated when necessary.
This strategy has been shown to yield high response rates and reduce nonresponse bias in prospective studies (De Leeuw, 2005 , 2018; Dillman et al., 2014; Sanchez-García et al., 2021).
text.formatted: This strategy has been shown to yield high response rates and reduce nonresponse bias in prospective studies <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(De Leeuw, 2005</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Dillman et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Sanchez-García et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Data collection and compensation procedures for participants were identical to those at baseline.
The study protocol (PID2020-118229RB-100) was approved by the Regional Research Bioethics Committee (Consejería de Salud, Andalucía, Spain).
Of the 612 participants assessed at baseline, 505 (82.5%) completed the 3-month follow-up.

Analyses of SAC avoidance included participants who reported past-month use of both alcohol and cannabis at baseline and follow-up (n = 382), and analyses of DUIC avoidance included participants who reported past-month cannabis use and driving at both time points (n = 167).
Table 1 presents the sociodemographic characteristics of follow-up completers and both analytical samples.

text.text: Age, sex, university student status, sexual orientation, primary source of income, and living arrangements were assessed at baseline.
Participants reported the number of days of alcohol use, cannabis use, SAC use, and DUIC in the past 30 days.

Perceived descriptive norms were assessed with the same two items were used to assess how often participants believed their typical cannabis-using peers had engaged in each behavior during the past month on a 6-point Likert scale (1 = never to6 = always).
Higher scores reflected stronger perceived descriptive norms.
Self-efficacy was assessed using the 3-item measure developed by Fernández-Calderón et al. (2025) in accordance with Ajzen's guidelines (Ajzen, 2006 (Ajzen, , 2013)).
text.formatted: Self-efficacy was assessed using the 3-item measure developed by <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Fernández-Calderón et al. (2025)</ref> in accordance with Ajzen's guidelines <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Ajzen, 2006</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Ajzen, , 2013))</ref>.

text.text: The measure was adapted for each target behavior (e.g., "If I wanted to, I would be able to avoid mixing cannabis and alcohol"; "If I wanted to, I could easily avoid driving after using cannabis").
Participants agree on a 7-point scale (1 = strongly disagree,7 = strongly agree).
Scores were computed by summing the three items for each behavior.
Internal consistency was adequate (α = .87 for SAC; α = .75 for DUIC).
Descriptive statistics and Pearson correlations were computed to examine the associations among the study variables.

Hierarchical multiple linear regression analyses were then conducted to examine the associations of descriptive norms and self-efficacy for avoiding SAC and DUIC, with separate models for each behavior and follow-up avoidance as the outcome variable.
Sex, age, and university student status and baseline frequency of the corresponding risk behavior (i.e., days of SAC or DUIC in the past month) were entered as covariates in Step 1.

University status was included give evidence that college students may be differentially exposed to substance use norms and risk behaviors relative to their non-college peers (Merrill & Carey, 2016; Sánchez-García et al., 2024), and baseline risk behavior was included to prior engagement in the specific behavior targeted by each protective outcome.

text.text: In Step 2, baseline descriptive norms and self-efficacy specific each behavior were entered.

Four participants in the SAC sample who identified with a sex other than male or female were excluded from all analyses including sex, give the insufficient size of this subgroup (n = 378); descriptive and correlational analyses were conducted with the full SAC sample (n = 382).

To examine the mediating role of self-efficacy, two simple mediation models were estimated for avoidance of SAC and DUIC using the PROCESS Model 4, with 5,000 bootstrapping resamples and 95% confidence intervals.

In both models, descriptive norms were specified as the predictor, self-efficacy as the mediator, and follow-up avoidance of the corresponding behavior as the outcome, controlling for the same covariates as in the regression analyses.
Finally, to examine whether sex moderated the mediating mechanism, moderated mediation analyses were conducted using PROCESS Model 59, with separate models for each behavior.

These models tested whether sex moderated (a) the association between descriptive norms and self-efficacy, (b) the association between self-efficacy and avoidance, and (c) the direct associations between descriptive norms and avoidance.
Conditional indirect effects for men and women, and the difference between them, were estimated using 5,000 bootstrap resamples and 95% confidence intervals.
Each model included the same covariates as the previous analyses, except sex, which was specified as the moderator.
Tables 2 present descriptive statistics and bivariate correlations for the SAC avoidance and DUIC avoidance samples.

For both samples, baseline descriptive norms were positively associated with baseline self-efficacy and with follow-up avoidance, and self-efficacy was positively associated with follow-up avoidance, with stronger associations for DUIC.
Hierarchical regression models are presented in Table 3.

text.text: The final models accounted for 11.1% and 30% of the variance in follow-up avoidance of SAC and DUIC, respectively.

In both models, the addition of descriptive norms and self-efficacy in Step 2 significantly increased the explained variance beyond sociodemographic covariates and baseline frequency of the risk behavior (ΔR² = .083 and .203).
Higher descriptive norms and higher self-efficacy were associated with greater subsequent avoidance of both behaviors.
Self-efficacy mediated the association between descriptive norms and avoidance of both behaviors (Figure 1).
text.formatted: Self-efficacy mediated the association between descriptive norms and avoidance of both behaviors (Figure <ref type="figure">1</ref>).

text.text: Higher baseline descriptive norms were associated with greater self-efficacy, which in turn was associated with greater avoidance at follow-up.

The indirect effect was significant for SAC (indirect effect = 0.021, 95% CI [0.001, 0.048]; Panel A) and DUIC (indirect effect = 0.062, 95% CI [0.015, 0.122]; Panel B), accounting for 7.1% and 14.7% of the total association, respectively.
Table 4 presents the moderated mediation models.

text.text: For SAC avoidance, sex did not moderate any of the associations examined, and the conditional indirect effects did not differ between men and women (difference = -0.035, 95% CI [-0.107, 0.019]).

For DUIC avoidance, sex moderated the direct association between descriptive norms and avoidance (b = 0.397, 95% CI [0.106, 0.688], p = .008), which was significant among men (b = 0.509, p < .001) but not among women (b = 0.112, p = .345; Figure 2).

text.text: Sex did not moderate the association between descriptive norms and self-efficacy (p = .059) or between self-efficacy and avoidance (p = .258), and the conditional indirect effects did not differ between men and women (difference = 0.033, 95% CI [-0.099, 0.140]).
Social cognitive theory suggests that observing peers who avoid risk behaviors may strengthen individuals' confidence in their own capacity to do the same.

Building on this premise, the present study examined the associations of descriptive norms and self-efficacy with subsequent avoidance of SAC and DUIC among young adults who use cannabis, the mediating role of self-efficacy in the association between norms and avoidance, and whether these associations differed by sex.
Descriptive norms and selfefficacy were associated with greater avoidance of both behaviors, and self-efficacy mediated the association between descriptive norms and avoidance in both cases.

Sex moderated only the direct association between descriptive norms and DUIC avoidance, which emerged among men but not women, whereas the indirect association through self-efficacy did not differ by sex.

Our findings are consistent with previous evidence identifying perceived descriptive norms as a relevant correlate of protective behaviors related to alcohol and cannabis use (e.g., Fernández-Calderón et al., 2022; Romero-Pérez et al., 2026), and extend it to two specific and particularly risk behaviors: the avoidance of SAC and DUIC.
text.formatted: Our findings are consistent with previous evidence identifying perceived descriptive norms as a relevant correlate of protective behaviors related to alcohol and cannabis use (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Fernández-Calderón et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Romero-Pérez et al., 2026)</ref>, and extend it to two specific and particularly risk behaviors: the avoidance of SAC and DUIC.

text.text: Notably, descriptive norms were the strongest correlate of the avoidance of both behaviors, even after accounting for baseline frequency of the corresponding risk behavior.
This may reflect the social nature of SAC and DUIC, which typically occur in group settings where peers' behavior is highly visible.

In addition, in contrast to studies using distal reference groups such as the typical student, norms in this study referred to the people with whom participants usually used cannabis, a proximal reference group that has been shown to be particularly influential in substance-related behaviors (Borsari & Carey, 2003; Fernández-Calderón et al., 2022).
text.formatted: In addition, in contrast to studies using distal reference groups such as the typical student, norms in this study referred to the people with whom participants usually used cannabis, a proximal reference group that has been shown to be particularly influential in substance-related behaviors <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Borsari & Carey, 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Fernández-Calderón et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Norm-based interventions, particularly personalized normative feedback, reduce alcohol use by correcting misperceptions about peers' behavior (Dotson et al., 2015; Lewis & Neighbors, 2006).

text.text: Given that young adults tend to underestimate their peers' use of protective strategies (Fernández-Calderón et al., 2022; Treat et al., 2025), similar approaches could be used to highlight that avoiding SAC and DUIC is common among peers, thereby promoting these behaviors as normative.

text.text: Self-efficacy was also associated with greater avoidance of both behaviors.

Although self-efficacy is a well-established correlate of substance refusal (Jang et al., 2013; Parrado-González et al., 2025), its role in substance-related protective behaviors has been less clear, with previous studies finding no association once other theory of planned behavior constructs were considered (Fernández-Calderón et al., 2025; Vera et al., 2025).

text.text: Our findings indicate that, beyond sociodemographic characteristics, baseline risk behavior, and descriptive norms, confidence in one's capacity to avoid SAC and DUIC is a relevant correlate of their subsequent avoidance, particularly for DUIC.

Avoiding DUIC may place greater demands on personal capacity, as it often requires planning alternatives in advance, such as arranging other transportation, and may be reinforced by awareness that cannabis impairs the skills needed to drive safely.
More importantly, self-efficacy mediated the association between descriptive norms and the avoidance of both behaviors.

This finding supports the social-cognitive premise that self-efficacy can be acquired through vicarious experience (Bandura, 1997; Conner & Norman, 2015): perceiving that the people with whom one uses cannabis avoid SAC and DUIC was associated with greater confidence in one's own capacity to avoid them, which in turn was associated with greater subsequent avoidance.

text.text: Experimental studies on other health behaviors, such as physical activity, have shown that descriptive norm information can increase self-efficacy (Priebe & Spink, 2014), and vicarious experience is among the intervention techniques most strongly associated with increases in self-efficacy (Ashford et al., 2010).

text.text: To our knowledge, this is the first study to document this mechanism for SAC and DUIC avoidance, suggesting that normative information may promote these behaviors not only by signaling what is common, but also by strengthening young adults' confidence in their ability to enact them.
Finally, sex moderated the direct association between descriptive norms and DUIC avoidance, which was significant among men but not among women, whereas no moderation was observed for SAC avoidance.

This finding is consistent with previous research showing stronger associations of descriptive norms with protective behavioral strategies (Romero-Pérez et al., 2026) and with DUIC intentions (Earle et al., 2020) among men than among women.

text.text: Gender norms may help explain this pattern, as young men's risk behaviors, including risky driving, tend to be more strongly influenced by peers (Brijs et al., 2022); thus, perceiving that peers avoid DUIC may carry greater weight in their decisions.

text.text: In contrast, the indirect association through self-efficacy did not differ by sex, which is compatible with the possibility that observational sources of self-efficacy, such as vicarious experience, operate similarly in men and women.

Accordingly, normative components may be particularly relevant for promoting DUIC avoidance among men, whereas strategies that build confidence in avoiding DUIC, such as planning alternative transportation in advance, may be useful regardless of sex.
This study has several limitations.
First, all variables were self-reported.

Social desirability may have led participants to overreport protective behaviors, and retrospective reports of the past month may be affected by recall bias; the latter could be reduced in future studies through ecological momentary assessment, which captures behaviors close to their occurrence (Stinson et al., 2022).

text.text: Second, the design does not permit causal conclusions.

Experimental or quasi-experimental studies, for example, interventions that manipulate normative information or explicitly strengthen selfefficacy, could examine the causal role of these mechanisms in promoting SAC and DUIC avoidance.
Third, the models focused on a limited set of psychosocial determinants, and future research could integrate other social-cognitive constructs, particularly attitudes.

Attitudes toward DUIC are often neutral or even positive, with many people who use cannabis believing that it does not impair, or even improves, their driving, in contrast to the negative attitudes generally held toward drink-driving (Boicu et al., 2024); such beliefs may reduce motivation to avoid DUIC.

text.text: Finally, the sample comprised young adults from two cities in southern Spain recruited through targeted sampling, a non-probabilistic procedure that limits representativeness; replication in larger and more diverse populations is needed to determine whether the observed associations hold across different social and cultural contexts.

This study provides prospective evidence that descriptive norms and selfefficacy are relevant correlates of subsequent SAC and DUIC avoidance among young adults who use cannabis, with descriptive norms showing the strongest association with avoidance of both behaviors.

Most notably, it is the first study to show that self-efficacy mediated the association between descriptive norms and the avoidance of these behaviors, suggesting that, as posited by social cognitive theory, perceiving that peers avoid SAC and DUIC may strengthen young adults' confidence in their own capacity to do the same.

Neither the association between norms and self-efficacy nor this indirect association differed significantly between men and women, whereas the direct association between norms and DUIC avoidance was observed only among men.

Prevention efforts could therefore use normative feedback to show that avoiding SAC and DUIC is common among peers, not only to correct misperceptions but also as a source of self-efficacy for both men and women, with particular attention to men in the case of DUIC.
